text: Everything you built in User Administration assumed local authentication without ever naming it. A user record lives in sys_user, with a username and a password hash, and when that user logs in, ServiceNow itself compares what they typed against what it stored. Single Sign-On, or SSO, changes who does that checking, and this lesson is about understanding exactly what shifts, and why large organizations almost always make that shift.

Under local authentication, ServiceNow is both the place the user works and the place that proves who they are. Under SSO, ServiceNow stops checking passwords entirely. Instead, it delegates that job to an external Identity Provider, or IdP, a system built to be the enterprise's one authentication chokepoint. When a user tries to log in, ServiceNow doesn't ask what's your password, it asks the IdP is this really them, and trusts the answer. The sys_user record still exists, because ServiceNow still needs to know who this person is for roles and groups, but the password field stops being the thing standing between a login attempt and access.

There are three real reasons enterprises make this move. Centralized password policy means one set of complexity and lockout rules at the IdP, inherited automatically by every connected application, instead of fifty separate policies across fifty systems. One login across the whole portfolio means employees authenticate once and move between every connected application without logging in again, a real reduction in help-desk tickets, not just a convenience. But offboarding is the argument that actually matters most. With local authentication, disabling a departing employee means remembering to separately disable their account in every application they ever touched. Miss one, and they still have a working login after they've left. With SSO, disabling one account at the IdP cuts off access to every connected system at once, including ServiceNow.

It's worth keeping this cleanly separate from Chapters 1 and 2. Roles, ACLs, and field-level security answer what someone's allowed to do once we know who they are. Authentication only answers how we know who they are in the first place. Moving to SSO changes nothing about role design, ACL evaluation order, or security_admin elevation. A user authenticated through an external IdP still gets exactly the roles their sys_user record and group memberships say they get. The two layers stack; neither replaces the other.

Local authentication means ServiceNow checks the password itself, which works but doesn't scale across a large application portfolio. SSO delegates that check to an external Identity Provider, and the offboarding argument alone usually settles the decision for any organization managing access across dozens of systems. Next up, the real protocol enterprises use to make SSO work: SAML-based SSO, and exactly how that trust between ServiceNow and an Identity Provider actually gets established.
